opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it was curiosity, and a bit of uncertainty too. When I started my PhD at UCSD, I didn't have a clear picture of what kind of researcher I wanted to be or what kind of environment suited me. The academic lab gives you one view of research: small group, a lot of freedom, you think deeply about a problem with your advisor. But I knew there were other ways of doing research, especially in industry labs, which at that time were becoming really important in computer vision and deep learning.

So I thought, why not use the summers to try different places? Each internship felt like a small experiment. I got to see how different organizations defined a "good problem," how they balanced long-term exploration against product impact, and how people collaborated. Some places were more engineering-driven, some were very open and academic in spirit. Being exposed to that variety helped me understand my own taste.

Another reason was the people. In research, who you work with matters enormously. Through internships I met mentors and peers I never would have crossed paths with otherwise, and some of those collaborations turned into really important work for me, and friendships that lasted long after.

Looking back, I'd say those internships were less about building a résumé and more about calibrating myself: figuring out what I cared about, what kind of research culture made me most productive, and eventually that shaped my decisions after the PhD as well.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he used internships to explore research environments and calibrate his preferences, but does not say he was testing whether something outside AI or computer vision might interest him more.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came from curiosity, and a bit of restlessness. When I was doing my PhD at UC San Diego with Zhuowen Tu, I was in a pretty small group, and I realized early on that academia, especially a single lab, gives you one particular lens on what research is and how it should be done. I wanted to see how other people did it.

So I interned at quite a few places: Adobe, NEC Labs, Google, Facebook AI Research. Each one was really a different culture. At Adobe, you see how research connects to actual products and what it means for an idea to survive contact with users. At NEC Labs it was closer to a traditional industrial lab, more focused and smaller. Google was enormous, with incredible infrastructure, and that taught me what it looks like when compute and engineering are basically not the bottleneck. And then FAIR, where I did my internship with Kaiming and Ross and Piotr, was something else entirely. It felt like an academic lab but with industry resources, and the standard for what counted as a good paper was extremely high.

What I took away was that there is no single correct way to do research. Some places optimize for breadth, some for depth, some for impact on a product. Seeing those tradeoffs made me much more deliberate about my own taste. I think the ResNeXt work, which came out of that FAIR internship, is a good example: it was simple, almost too simple, and in a different environment I might have been told it wasn't novel enough. But that group valued simplicity and clarity, and that resonated with me.

The other thing, frankly, is that internships are the cheapest way to try on a future. You get three months to find out whether you actually like working in that kind of place before you commit years to it. For me that was really valuable, because by the end of my PhD I knew pretty clearly that I wanted to be somewhere that felt like FAIR did, where you could still do fundamental work but with the resources to do it seriously.

astra-6.text:
I wanted to understand what it actually felt like to do research in different environments. During a PhD, you get to know your own lab very well, but that’s only one way of working. I was curious about how people elsewhere chose problems, collaborated, and balanced longer-term ideas with more immediate goals.

Internships seemed like a good way to explore that before deciding what to do after graduation. It wasn’t just about finding an interesting project; it was also about learning what kind of research environment would suit me, and challenging some of the assumptions I’d picked up in my own lab.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes exploring research environments and finding a suitable fit, but does not say Xie wanted to test whether another field might interest him more than AI or computer vision.

sol-6.1.text: For me, internships were a way to explore what doing research could look like beyond my PhD lab. I wanted to experience different environments, work with different people, and understand how they chose problems. You can learn a lot from papers, but working alongside someone gives you a much better sense of how they think. It was also a way to figure out what kind of environment would suit me after graduation.
